Forecasters predicting infectious disease outbreaks have met with varying success.
Some of that variation comes from the forecasting method used, and some from the difficulty of the target being forecast.
Separating the two is what identifies which factors can be modified to improve performance, and what performance to expect in a given setting.
Here we set out one approach to doing so, applied to forecasts of Covid-19 in Europe.

Performance is better under stable epidemic dynamics [@bracher2022], in larger populations [@lopez2024], where surveillance is timely and accurate [@reich2019; @holcomb2023], and where informative leading indicators exist [@delvalle2018].
It is consistently better at shorter horizons [@cramer2022], plausibly bounded by the serial interval linking disease to observation [@sherratt2023], prompting the suggestion that predictability is inherently limited by the complexity of the disease-surveillance-response system [@scarpino2019].

Performance also varies with the forecast estimation process: the structural approach and implementation choices behind each model.
Methods range from purely data-driven statistical models to mechanistic models embedding explicit hypotheses about transmission, and different structures suit different purposes, such as scenario projection, policy analysis, or nowcasting [@woolhouse2011; @dattner2018; @funk2020].
Comparisons between structures have found little evidence of differences in predictive performance [@carlson2018; @viboud2018; @reich2019].

Realised performance therefore combines two processes (@fig-processes), which must be separated to compare forecasters fairly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-processes
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Two processes generating variation in predictive performance, with examples of factors contributing to each process.
#|   Factors that generate the forecast (e.g. model specification), and factors that generate the target (e.g. epidemic dynamics) may each contribute to realised predictive performance.

DiagrammeR::grViz('
digraph processes {
  graph [rankdir = TB, fontname = "inherit", bgcolor = "white"]
  node  [shape = box, style = filled, fillcolor = "white",
         color = "black", fontcolor = "black", fontname = "inherit"]
  edge  [color = "black"]

  subgraph cluster_FG {
    label = "Forecast-generating process"; color = "black"; fontcolor = "black"
    F1 [label = "Modeller participation"]
    F2 [label = "Model specification"]
    F3 [label = "Model implementation"]
  }
  subgraph cluster_TG {
    label = "Target-generating process"; color = "black"; fontcolor = "black"
    T1 [label = "Epidemic dynamics"]
    T2 [label = "Observation process"]
    T3 [label = "Target specification"]
  }
  F [label = "Forecast"]
  T [label = "Target"]
  P [label = "Predictive performance"]

  F1 -> F; F2 -> F; F3 -> F
  F -> P
  T1 -> T; T2 -> T; T3 -> T
  T -> P
}
')
```

Comparable samples of many independent models across many targets come from participatory forecast challenges, which collate predictions for pre-specified targets in a standardised format [@pollett2020; @reich2022].
Such comparisons are prone to selection bias and confounding, because forecasters participate differentially across targets: aggregated comparisons conflate the performance of a modelling approach with the difficulty of the targets it was applied to.

Evaluators have borrowed, mostly implicitly, from observational research to control this bias (@tbl-approaches).
Epidemiology separates tools applied when a study is designed, such as restriction and matching, from those applied to data already collected, such as stratification, standardisation and regression adjustment [@mcnamee2005; @kahlert2017].
In forecast evaluation that distinction largely collapses, since the evaluator almost always works with forecasts already submitted.
The exception is differential participation, which a protocol requiring every model to forecast every target would remove at the point of collection, but that is available to hub organisers rather than to anyone evaluating afterwards.
@tbl-approaches is therefore restricted to retrospective tools, ordered by the stage of the analysis at which each acts.
Among the elements governing how units are compared, from matching through to regression adjustment, that order is also one of increasing formality.
It does not extend to the whole table: complete ascertainment and unbiased classification of the exposure are prerequisites to any comparison rather than weaker forms of it.
The simpler tools may not isolate a single component of performance when variation is large across both many targets and many models.

| Study design element | In observational research | In forecast evaluation | Threat addressed | Limitation |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| Inclusion criteria | Exclude units with particular covariate values so the covariate cannot vary | Exclude targets whose observed data were revised after forecasts were made [@sherratt2023]; or exclude models below a submission threshold | Confounding, selection | Loses power; narrows the population the estimate applies to |
| Measurement of exposure | Classify exposure without sight of the outcome, and report agreement between assessors | Classify the model characteristic under comparison from submitted metadata, with the classifier blind to scores | Information | Metadata are self-reported and thin; misclassification remains, and attenuates effects toward the null |
| Scale of outcome | Express the outcome so it does not depend on a nuisance quantity: rates rather than counts, or ratios rather than differences | Score forecasts per 100,000 population, and on the log scale so the score reflects relative rather than absolute error [@bosse2022; @bosse2023] | Confounding by population size and by incidence magnitude | Removes the dependence by redefining what is measured, not by adjusting for it; the quantity compared is no longer error on the natural scale |
| Unadjusted comparison | Report the crude association between exposure and outcome, with no control | Rank models, or compare mean scores between structures, over all forecasts as submitted | None | Conflates the method used with the difficulty of the targets each model chose to forecast |
| Matching on covariates | Pair exposed and unexposed units on covariate values | Compare forecasters only on targets both submitted for [@bracher2021] | Confounding | Sparse overlap; the estimate holds only for the matched set |
| Stratification | Estimate the association within levels of a covariate, then pool | Report scores by horizon, location, or epidemic phase [@reich2019; @cramer2022] | Confounding | Cells sparse and uneven with several interacting factors; continuous covariates need arbitrary binning |
| Indirect standardisation | Compare observed events against those expected under a reference rate, as in a standardised mortality ratio | Relative skill against a naive baseline model available for all targets [@bracher2021] | Confounding by target difficulty | Interpretable only against the chosen reference, which materially changes rankings [@stapper] |
| Regression adjustment | Enter covariates in a model; read the partial association | Estimate the partial effect of model structure adjusting for outcome, incidence, trend, variant, country, horizon, and model | Confounding, clustering | Specification-dependent; the estimand is not formally defined |
| Quantitative bias analysis | Derive a minimal sufficient adjustment set from a directed acyclic graph [@hernan2020]; bound unmeasured confounding with an E-value [@vanderweele2017] | Not yet applied in forecast evaluation | Residual confounding | Requires metadata and sample size that current hubs do not provide |

: Approaches to controlling bias in comparative forecast evaluation, with analogous tools from observational study design. Rows follow the sequence of analysis: what enters the sample, measurement of exposure and outcome, comparison across units of observation, and estimation. {#tbl-approaches}

Model structure is further entangled with strategy.
A forecaster may produce forecasts for any target from updated data alone, as statistical time-series and many semi-mechanistic models do, or tailor a model to the data-generating process of a specific target.
Strategy may therefore influence performance separately, confounding the effect of structure.

Here we estimate the partial effect of model structure on predictive performance, while jointly adjusting for factors contributing to target difficulty.
We score short-term Covid-19 forecasts across Europe with proper scoring rules, and model them with a generalised additive mixed model accounting for the epidemiological outcome, trend and level of incidence, dominant variant phase, country, forecast horizon, and individual model.
Pooling across sparse, interacting subgroups by partial shrinkage avoids stratifying them, and continuous sources of difficulty enter as smooth functions.
A directed acyclic graph in the Supplement sets out our assumptions; this work is exploratory rather than formally causal.
We find most variation in observed performance is associated with the forecast target rather than the forecasting method, and argue for a wider range of evaluative study designs.
